explanations.answer: It will be raised above the hills
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD "will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills" (Micah 4:1). Micah has just talked about Zion being plowed like a field (Micah 3:12), so this is a big turn. The mountain goes from plowed over to lifted up.

explanations.answer: It will be split down the middle
explanations.explanation: Splitting a mountain is a real thing in the Bible, but it's not what Micah says here. He says the mountain of the house of the LORD "will be established as the chief of the mountains" (Micah 4:1). Nothing gets cracked in half. It gets raised above the hills, friend.

explanations.answer: It will be covered in thick cloud
explanations.explanation: Clouds are a nice guess, but Micah doesn't mention any. He says the mountain "will be raised above the hills, and the peoples will stream to it" (Micah 4:1). Folks can't stream toward something they can't see, so I think a clear view fits. Micah's point is the lifting up, and the peoples coming.

Right on the money, baker. The nations say, "He will teach us His ways, so that we may walk in His paths" (Micah 4:2). They're not showing up to be impressive. They're showing up to learn. I respect that, because I'm still learning things in my own bakery.

Forgiveness is wonderful, but it's not what these nations ask for. They say, "He will teach us His ways, so that we may walk in His paths" (Micah 4:2). Kings never even come up in their words. They want to be taught, friend.

Nobody in this crowd is asking for real estate, baker. They say, "He will teach us His ways, so that we may walk in His paths" (Micah 4:2). They're climbing the mountain to learn, not to move in. No moving boxes needed for this trip.

Plowshares is the word. "Then they will beat their swords into plowshares" (Micah 4:3). A plowshare is the blade of a plow, so a weapon becomes a farming tool. Same metal, brand new job. I know a little about that, baker.

A shield is still gear for a fight, and Micah goes the other way. "Then they will beat their swords into plowshares" (Micah 4:3). A plowshare is the blade of a plow. So the swords get hammered into farm tools, friend, not more battle gear.

Arrowheads would just be a different way to keep fighting, baker. Micah says, "Then they will beat their swords into plowshares" (Micah 4:3). A plowshare is the blade of a plow, made for dirt and not for war. The swords stop being swords.

Not quite, baker. The verse says the opposite: "Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor will they train anymore for war" (Micah 4:3). Once the swords are plowshares, the fighting stops. Not even practice rounds, friend.

False is right. Micah says, "Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor will they train anymore for war" (Micah 4:3). No fighting and no practicing for it either. That's a whole lot of retired war gear.

You got it, baker. Each man sits under his own vine and fig tree, "with no one to frighten him" (Micah 4:4). He's not looking over his shoulder. I spent years in the dark listening for the drawer to open, so I know a calm seat is a gift.

Micah never says the work runs out, friend. He says each man will sit under his own vine and fig tree, "with no one to frighten him" (Micah 4:4). What's missing is the fear. A vine and a fig tree sounds like a place with plenty going on.

Neighbors aren't part of what's missing, baker. The verse says each man sits under his own vine and fig tree, "with no one to frighten him" (Micah 4:4). The only thing gone is the fear. I think neighbors are welcome. Somebody has to share the figs.

That's the one, baker. Micah says, "Though all the nations may walk in the name of their gods, yet we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever" (Micah 4:5). Other crowds go their own ways, but this "we" stays put. Forever and ever is a long time to be faithful.

There's no side-by-side walking in this verse, friend. It says, "Though all the nations may walk in the name of their gods, yet we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever" (Micah 4:5). That "yet" marks the difference. The ones who say "our God" walk with the LORD.

explanations.answer: Walk their own way for now
explanations.explanation: "For now" is the trouble with this one, baker. Micah says, "yet we will walk in the name of the LORD our God forever and ever" (Micah 4:5). Forever and ever doesn't have an expiration date. Even my cookies have a better shelf life than "for now."

Outcast, yes. The LORD says, "I will gather the lame; I will assemble the outcast" (Micah 4:6). Those are the folks He's picking up on that day. I've been in the back of a drawer, so that hits home for me, baker.

The proud aren't on this list, baker. The LORD says, "I will gather the lame; I will assemble the outcast" (Micah 4:6). He's gathering the ones who got pushed to the edges. The proud just aren't in this verse.

The mighty don't show up here, friend. The LORD says, "I will gather the lame; I will assemble the outcast" (Micah 4:6). He starts with the ones who got left out. I'd say that's good news for anyone who's ever felt overlooked.

Strong is right, baker. The LORD says, "I will make the lame into a remnant, the outcast into a strong nation" (Micah 4:7). The ones on the edge become a strong nation. I once got picked out of a drawer for a big job, so I love hearing it.

Scattered is the opposite of what He's doing, baker. The LORD says, "I will gather the lame" and then makes "the outcast into a strong nation" (Micah 4:6-7). He's gathering, not spreading folks out. Think of it as one big batch, not crumbs across the counter.

Hidden doesn't fit, friend. The LORD says, "I will make the lame into a remnant, the outcast into a strong nation" (Micah 4:7). Nothing about staying out of sight. Anybody can tell a strong nation when they see one.
True, baker. The verse says, "Then the LORD will rule over them in Mount Zion from that day and forever" (Micah 4:7). It starts that day and never stops. That's a ruler worth sticking with.
Careful on this one, friend. Micah 4:7 says, "Then the LORD will rule over them in Mount Zion from that day and forever." So the statement is true. His rule starts that day and keeps going forever.
Restored, baker! The LORD says, "the former dominion will be restored to you" (Micah 4:8). Something that was lost comes back. I know that feeling, and it is a good one.
Forgotten is the opposite of the promise, friend. The LORD says, "the former dominion will be restored to you" (Micah 4:8). Nobody's getting lost in the dust here. It's all coming back.

Removed would be bad news, baker, and this is good news. The LORD says, "the former dominion will be restored to you; sovereignty will come to the Daughter of Jerusalem" (Micah 4:8). Nothing gets taken away. It comes back to her.
